ety.text: From Middle English puple, peple, peeple, from Anglo-Norman people, from Old French pueple, peuple, pople, from Latin populus (“a people, nation”), from Old Latin populus, from earlier poplus, from even earlier poplos, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”) of unknown origin. Doublet of pueblo. Gradually ousted native English lede and, partially, folk. Originally used with singular verbs (e.g.
From Middle English peplen, peuplien, partly from Middle French peupler (from peuple (“people”)) and partly from the noun (etymology 1).

senses.d: Persons forming or belonging to a particular group, such as a nation, class, ethnic group, country, family, etc.
ex: a people apart
an industrious people

senses.d: A group of persons regarded as being servants, followers, companions or subjects of a ruler or leader.
ex: Moses said, "Let my people go."
his people were weary
I'll have my people call your people.
I have my people working on it.

senses.d: A person's ancestors, relatives or family.
ex: My people lived through the Black Plague and the Thirty Years War.
His people live out west.

senses.d: The mass of a community as distinguished from a special class (elite); the commonalty; the populace; the vulgar; the common crowd; the citizens.
ex: The people have successfully stood up against tyranny and totalitarianism.
The election is over and the people have spoken.

senses.d: People in general, humans, by extension sentient beings real or fictional.
ex: People don't like it when you tweak their noses.
Teachers are people too.

senses.d: To interact with people; to socialize.
ex:
My head tilted as Calvin said, "Don't worry about him. He just doesn't people well.
The fuck? I people. Sometimes. With people I know.
I don't people well.” He laughed at that. “You do okay,” he assured her.

senses.d: To stock with people or inhabitants; to fill as with people; to populate.
ex: He would not be alone, who all things can; / But peopled Heav'n with Angels, Earth with Man.

senses.d: To inhabit; to occupy; to populate.
ex: […] / As thick and numberless / As the gay motes that people the Sun Beams, / […]
